grammarLessons.title: Present Simple Tense
grammarLessons.description: Learn the present simple tense: structure, positive and negative sentences, questions, examples and common mistakes.
grammarLessons.definition: The present simple tense describes habits, routines, general truths and fixed schedules. It is the tense you use most when talking about yourself and your daily life.
rules: With I, you, we and they, use the base verb: I work, they play.
With he, she, it or one person, add -s or -es: she works, he watches.
Verbs ending in consonant + y change y to -ies: study → studies.
For negatives and questions, use do or does with the base verb. Never add -s twice.
Common time words: always, usually, often, sometimes, never, every day, on Mondays.

examples.sentence: I drink tea every morning.
She works in a hospital.
The train leaves at 7:30 a.m.
Water boils at 100°C.

sections.heading: Negative sentences
sections.structure: Subject + do not / does not + base verb

examples.sentence: I don't eat meat.
He doesn't like cold weather.
examples.note: does already shows he/she/it, so like has no -s

examples.sentence: They don't live in Mumbai.
Do you speak Hindi? Yes, I do.
Does she play the guitar? No, she doesn't.
Where do they work?

sections.heading: Spelling of he / she / it forms
sections.body: Most verbs add -s. Verbs ending in -s, -sh, -ch, -x or -o add -es. Consonant + y becomes -ies. Have is irregular: he has.

examples.sentence: play → plays, read → reads
watch → watches, go → goes, fix → fixes
study → studies, carry → carries

mistakes.wrong: She go to college by bus.
mistakes.right: She goes to college by bus.
mistakes.why: With she, add -es to go.
After does, use the base verb.
Know is a state verb; it is not used in the continuous form.
Use does not with he, she and it.

practice.explanation: She takes the -es form: she goes.
Negative with he/she/it: does not + base verb.
Parents is plural (they), so use do.

grammarLessons.title: Present Continuous Tense
grammarLessons.description: Use the present continuous for actions happening now and temporary situations, with clear examples and practice.
grammarLessons.definition: The present continuous describes actions happening right now, temporary situations and fixed future plans.
rules: Form it with am / is / are + verb-ing.
Use it for now: now, right now, at the moment, look!, listen!
Use it for temporary situations: I'm staying with my aunt this month.
Use it for future arrangements: We're meeting the client tomorrow.
State verbs (know, like, want, believe) are not normally used in the continuous.

examples.sentence: I am reading a novel.
Look! It's raining.
They are building a new metro line.

sections.heading: Negatives and questions
sections.structure: Subject + am/is/are + not + verb-ing  ·  Am/Is/Are + subject + verb-ing?

examples.sentence: She isn't working today.
Are you listening to me?
What are you cooking?

mistakes.wrong: I am wanting a new phone.
mistakes.why: Want is a state verb.
The helping verb is/am/are is required.

grammarLessons.title: Past Simple Tense
grammarLessons.description: Learn the past simple tense with regular and irregular verbs, negatives, questions and common mistakes.
grammarLessons.definition: The past simple describes completed actions at a specific time in the past.
rules: Regular verbs add -ed: work → worked, play → played.
Irregular verbs have special forms: go → went, eat → ate, buy → bought.
Negatives and questions use did + base verb: I didn't go. Did you go?
Common time words: yesterday, last week, in 2019, two days ago.

examples.sentence: We visited Jaipur last year.
He bought a new laptop yesterday.

sections.heading: Negatives and questions
sections.structure: Subject + did not + base verb  ·  Did + subject + base verb?

examples.sentence: I didn't see him at the party.
Did you finish the report?

mistakes.right: I didn't go to the office.
mistakes.why: After did, use the base verb.
Finished time (yesterday) takes the past simple.

practice.prompt: ___ you call your mother last night?
practice.explanation: Past simple question: Did + subject + base verb.

grammarLessons.title: Present Perfect Tense
grammarLessons.description: Understand the present perfect: have/has + past participle, since and for, and when not to use it.
grammarLessons.definition: The present perfect connects the past with the present: life experiences, recent actions with a present result, and situations that started in the past and continue now.
rules: Form it with have / has + past participle (V3).
Use since with a point in time (since 2020) and for with a period (for three years).
Use already, yet, just, ever and never with this tense.
Do not use it with finished time words like yesterday or last year.

examples.sentence: I have lived in Pune since 2018.
She has just finished her exam.
Have you ever been to Kerala?
We haven't received the parcel yet.

mistakes.wrong: I am living here since five years.
mistakes.right: I have lived here for five years.
mistakes.why: Use present perfect with for/since; five years is a period, so use for.
Use the past participle (gone), not the past form (went).

practice.explanation: Since + point in time → present perfect.

grammarLessons.title: Countable and Uncountable Nouns
grammarLessons.description: Learn the difference between countable and uncountable nouns, with much/many, some/any and common mistakes.
grammarLessons.definition: Countable nouns can be counted (one book, two books). Uncountable nouns cannot be counted and have no plural (water, advice, information).
rules: Countable nouns take a/an in the singular and -s in the plural.
Uncountable nouns never take a/an or -s.
Use many with countable and much with uncountable nouns.
Use a piece of, a cup of, a glass of to count uncountable things.

sections.heading: Common uncountable nouns
sections.body: advice, information, luggage, furniture, news, money, water, rice, bread, homework, equipment, traffic.

examples.sentence: How many students are in your class?
How much money do you need?
Can I give you a piece of advice?

mistakes.right: She gave me a lot of information.
mistakes.why: Information is uncountable.

mistakes.wrong: I have a lot of homeworks.
mistakes.right: I have a lot of homework.
mistakes.why: Homework is uncountable.

practice.explanation: Luggage is uncountable, so use much.

grammarLessons.title: Singular and Plural Nouns
grammarLessons.description: Spelling rules for plural nouns, including -s, -es, -ies and irregular plurals like children and people.
grammarLessons.definition: A singular noun means one; a plural noun means more than one. Most plurals add -s, but there are some spelling rules and irregular forms.
rules: Most nouns add -s: car → cars.
Nouns ending in -s, -x, -ch, -sh add -es: bus → buses, box → boxes.
Consonant + y becomes -ies: city → cities.
Irregular: man → men, woman → women, child → children, person → people, foot → feet.

examples.sentence: There are three churches in this area.
Two women and five children are waiting.

mistakes.why: People is already plural.

grammarLessons.title: Subject, Object and Possessive Pronouns
grammarLessons.description: Master I/me/my/mine, he/him/his and other pronouns with clear tables and examples.
grammarLessons.definition: Pronouns replace nouns so we do not repeat them. Their form changes depending on their job in the sentence.
rules: Subject pronouns do the action: I, you, he, she, it, we, they.
Object pronouns receive the action: me, you, him, her, it, us, them.
Possessive adjectives come before a noun: my, your, his, her, its, our, their.
Possessive pronouns stand alone: mine, yours, his, hers, ours, theirs.

examples.sentence: She called me yesterday.
This is my bag. That one is yours.
The company changed its logo.

mistakes.why: Use the subject pronoun I, and put yourself last.
It's means it is.

practice.explanation: Possessive pronoun stands alone at the end.

grammarLessons.title: Modal Verbs: can, should, must
grammarLessons.description: Use can, could, should, must and might for ability, advice, rules and possibility.
grammarLessons.definition: Modal verbs are helping verbs that add meaning such as ability, permission, advice, obligation or possibility.
rules: A modal is followed by the base verb with no to: She can swim.
Modals never take -s: He should rest (not shoulds).
Questions put the modal first: Can you help me?
Negatives add not: You mustn't smoke here.

examples.sentence: I can speak three languages.
Could you open the window, please?
You should drink more water.
Passengers must wear seat belts.
It might rain later.

mistakes.why: No to after a modal.

practice.prompt: You look tired. You ___ go to bed early.

grammarLessons.title: Irregular Verbs You Need First
grammarLessons.description: The 30 most useful irregular verbs with base, past and past participle forms and example sentences.
grammarLessons.definition: Irregular verbs do not form the past with -ed. You need to learn their past (V2) and past participle (V3) forms.
rules: Learn verbs in groups that change the same way.
Practise all three forms together: go – went – gone.
Use V2 for past simple and V3 after have/has/had.

sections.heading: Same in all forms
sections.body: cut – cut – cut, put – put – put, let – let – let, cost – cost – cost

sections.heading: V2 and V3 the same
sections.body: buy – bought – bought, teach – taught – taught, find – found – found, make – made – made

sections.heading: All different
sections.body: go – went – gone, eat – ate – eaten, write – wrote – written, speak – spoke – spoken, see – saw – seen

mistakes.why: After have, use V3 (written).

practice.prompt: Past participle of “speak”: I have ___ to the manager.

grammarLessons.title: Comparatives and Superlatives
grammarLessons.description: Compare things with -er/-est and more/most, including irregular forms like better and best.
grammarLessons.definition: Use comparatives to compare two things and superlatives to compare three or more.
rules: Short adjectives add -er / -est: tall → taller → the tallest.
Long adjectives use more / most: expensive → more expensive → the most expensive.
Irregular: good → better → best, bad → worse → worst, far → farther → farthest.
Use than after a comparative: Delhi is bigger than Pune.

examples.sentence: This phone is cheaper than that one.
Mount Everest is the highest mountain in the world.
Her English is better than mine.

mistakes.wrong: He is more taller than me.
mistakes.why: Don't use more with -er.

practice.prompt: This is the ___ day of my life.

grammarLessons.title: Adverbs of Frequency
grammarLessons.description: Always, usually, often, sometimes, rarely, never: what they mean and where they go in a sentence.
grammarLessons.definition: Adverbs of frequency tell us how often something happens.
rules: Put them before the main verb: I often walk to work.
Put them after be: She is always on time.
Sometimes can also go at the start: Sometimes I cook.

sections.heading: From 100% to 0%
sections.body: always (100%) → usually → often → sometimes → rarely → never (0%)

mistakes.wrong: I go always to the gym.
mistakes.right: I always go to the gym.
mistakes.why: Frequency adverbs go before the main verb.

grammarLessons.title: A, An and The
grammarLessons.description: Choose between a, an, the and no article using the vowel-sound rule, with examples and common mistakes.
grammarLessons.definition: A and an mean one or any. The means a specific thing both speakers know about.
rules: Use a before a consonant sound: a book, a university.
Use an before a vowel sound: an apple, an hour, an MBA.
Use the for something specific or unique: the sun, the book on the table.
Use no article for general plurals and uncountables: I love music.

examples.sentence: She is an engineer.
I saw a dog. The dog was very friendly.
Life is beautiful.

mistakes.why: Jobs need a/an.
Abstract ideas in general take no article.

grammarLessons.title: In, On and At for Time and Place
grammarLessons.description: Learn when to use in, on and at for time and place with a simple big-to-small rule.
grammarLessons.definition: In, on and at show time and place. Think of them as moving from big (in) to specific (at).
rules: Time: in for months, years, seasons (in May); on for days and dates (on Monday); at for clock times (at 6 p.m.).
Place: in for enclosed spaces and cities (in the room, in Chennai); on for surfaces (on the table); at for points (at the bus stop).
Fixed phrases: at night, in the morning, on the weekend (US) / at the weekend (UK).

examples.sentence: My birthday is on 14 March.
The meeting is at 3:30.
She lives in Hyderabad.

mistakes.why: Days take on.

grammarLessons.title: And, But, So, Because
grammarLessons.description: Join sentences with and, but, so and because to sound more fluent.
grammarLessons.definition: Conjunctions join words and ideas. These four are the most common in everyday English.
rules: and adds information
but shows contrast
so shows a result
because gives a reason

examples.sentence: I was hungry, so I made a sandwich.
The hotel was small but clean.
She stayed home because she was ill.

mistakes.wrong: Because I was tired. I slept early.
mistakes.right: I slept early because I was tired.
mistakes.why: A because-clause needs a main clause.

practice.prompt: It was raining, ___ we took an umbrella.

grammarLessons.title: Basic Word Order (S + V + O)
grammarLessons.description: Build correct English sentences with subject–verb–object order, and form negatives and questions.
grammarLessons.definition: Most English sentences follow Subject + Verb + Object. Place and time usually come at the end.
rules: Statement: Ravi drinks tea every morning.
Negative: Ravi doesn't drink tea.
Yes/No question: Does Ravi drink tea?
Wh- question: What does Ravi drink?

sections.heading: Order of extra information
sections.body: Subject + Verb + Object + Place + Time: I met my friends at the café yesterday.

mistakes.why: In questions, the helping verb comes before the subject.

options: I every day read the newspaper.
I read the newspaper every day.
Read I the newspaper every day.
The newspaper I read every day.
practice.answer: I read the newspaper every day.

grammarLessons.title: Passive Voice Basics
grammarLessons.description: Learn how to form the passive voice in different tenses and when to use it.
grammarLessons.definition: In the passive voice, the object of the action becomes the subject. We use it when the action is more important than who did it.
rules: Form: be + past participle (V3).
Present: The rooms are cleaned every day.
Past: The bridge was built in 1990.
Add by + doer only when it is important: The novel was written by R. K. Narayan.

examples.sentence: Active: Someone stole my bike. → Passive: My bike was stolen.
Active: They will announce the results. → Passive: The results will be announced.

mistakes.why: Use V3 after be.

grammarLessons.title: Reported Statements
grammarLessons.description: Change direct speech to indirect speech with the right tense shifts and pronoun changes.
grammarLessons.definition: Indirect (reported) speech tells someone what another person said, without quoting their exact words.
rules: The tense usually moves one step back: am → was, will → would, has done → had done.
Pronouns change to fit the reporter: “I am tired,” she said → She said she was tired.
Time words change: today → that day, tomorrow → the next day.
Say + (that); tell + person + (that).

examples.sentence: “I live in Goa.” → He said he lived in Goa.
“I will call you.” → She told me she would call me.

mistakes.wrong: He said me that he was busy.
mistakes.right: He told me that he was busy.
mistakes.why: Tell takes a person; say does not.

practice.prompt: “I am hungry,” said Arjun. → Arjun said that he ___ hungry.

vocabularyWords.meaning: A short trip to do a small job, such as buying something or posting a letter.
examples: I need to run a few errands before dinner.
She sent her son on an errand to the pharmacy.

vocabularyWords.meaning: To travel regularly between your home and your place of work or study.
examples: I commute to the office by metro.
His daily commute takes an hour each way.

vocabularyWords.meaning: Arriving or doing something at exactly the expected time.
examples: Our teacher is always punctual.
Please be punctual for the interview.

vocabularyWords.meaning: To discuss something formally in order to reach an agreement.
examples: We negotiated a better price with the supplier.
The union is negotiating a new contract.

vocabularyWords.meaning: The total income a company receives from its business activities.
examples: The company's revenue grew by 20% this year.
Advertising is their main source of revenue.

vocabularyWords.meaning: The latest time or date by which something must be finished.
examples: The deadline for applications is 30 June.
We worked late to meet the deadline.

vocabularyWords.meaning: A detailed plan of a journey, including places and times.
examples: Our itinerary includes two days in Udaipur.
The travel agent emailed me the itinerary.

vocabularyWords.meaning: The bags and suitcases you carry when you travel.
examples: Please do not leave your luggage unattended.
How much luggage can I take on the flight?

vocabularyWords.meaning: The place someone is travelling to.
examples: Goa is a popular holiday destination.
We reached our destination after six hours.

vocabularyWords.meaning: The subjects and content taught in a school, college or course.
examples: Coding is now part of the school curriculum.
The curriculum covers grammar and speaking.

vocabularyWords.meaning: To study again something you have already learned, especially before an exam.
examples: I need to revise for my English test.
She revises a little every evening.

vocabularyWords.meaning: Showing care and steady effort in your work or studies.
examples: Diligent students practise every day.
He is a diligent and reliable employee.

vocabularyWords.meaning: Having a very pleasant taste or smell.
examples: This biryani is delicious!
The bakery sells delicious cakes.

vocabularyWords.meaning: One of the foods used to make a dish.
examples: The main ingredients are rice, lentils and spices.
Check the ingredients if you have an allergy.

vocabularyWords.meaning: The feeling of wanting to eat.
examples: Walking in the fresh air gave me an appetite.
He has lost his appetite since he got sick.

vocabularyWords.meaning: To copy data or a file from the internet to your device.
examples: Download the app to practise offline.
The file is too large to download.

vocabularyWords.meaning: A machine or tool made for a particular purpose, such as a phone or tablet.
examples: Please switch off all electronic devices.
You can use English-Bridgeway on any device.

vocabularyWords.meaning: Using new methods or ideas.
examples: The startup has an innovative approach to learning.
We need innovative solutions to this problem.

vocabularyWords.meaning: Feeling or showing thanks for something someone has done.
examples: I'm grateful for your help.
We are grateful to all our volunteers.

vocabularyWords.meaning: Worried and nervous about something that might happen.
examples: She felt anxious before her interview.
Don't be anxious; you're well prepared.

vocabularyWords.meaning: Feeling that you have too much to deal with.
examples: I felt overwhelmed by the amount of work.
She was overwhelmed with joy at the news.

vocabularyWords.meaning: A brother or sister.
examples: I have two siblings, a brother and a sister.
Siblings often argue but stay close.

vocabularyWords.meaning: The parents and relatives of your husband or wife.
examples: We're visiting my in-laws this weekend.
She gets along well with her in-laws.

vocabularyWords.meaning: The way a child is cared for and taught while growing up.
examples: He had a strict but loving upbringing.
Our upbringing shapes our values.

vocabularyWords.meaning: A person you work with.
examples: My colleague helped me with the presentation.
I had lunch with a few colleagues.

vocabularyWords.meaning: A move to a higher position or rank at work.
examples: She got a promotion after two years.
Hard work led to his promotion.

vocabularyWords.meaning: To give part of your work or responsibility to someone else.
examples: A good manager knows how to delegate.
I delegated the report to my assistant.

spokenLessons.title: Introducing Yourself
spokenLessons.situation: Meeting a new classmate on the first day of an English course.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.text: Hi, what's your name?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.name: Rahul
dialogue.text: Hi, my name is Rahul. Nice to meet you.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.text: Nice to meet you too. I'm Priya. Where are you from?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.name: Rahul
dialogue.text: I'm from Nashik, but I live in Pune now. I work as a software tester.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.text: Oh, interesting! Why are you learning English?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.name: Rahul
dialogue.text: I want to speak more confidently in meetings. How about you?

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.name: Priya
dialogue.text: I'm preparing for job interviews. I hope we can practise together!

phrases.meaning: A polite thing to say when you meet someone for the first time.

phrases.phrase: I'm from … but I live in … now.
phrases.meaning: Say where you grew up and where you live.
Return the question to keep the conversation going.

activity: Record a 30-second introduction with your name, city, job or studies and one hobby.
Replace “Myself Rahul” with “I'm Rahul” every time you introduce yourself this week.

spokenLessons.title: Greeting People at Different Times
spokenLessons.situation: Meeting a neighbour in the morning and an old friend in the evening.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.name: Mrs Kulkarni
dialogue.text: Good morning, Aman! Off to college?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.name: Aman
dialogue.text: Good morning, aunty! Yes, I have an early class today.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.name: Mrs Kulkarni
dialogue.text: Have a good day!

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.name: Aman
dialogue.text: Thank you, you too!

phrases.meaning: Formal greetings by time of day.
Informal: you haven't met for a long time.
Casual way to ask how someone is.
A friendly way to say goodbye.

vocabulary.meaning: a person who lives near you

activity: Greet three people today using a different greeting each time.
Remember: “Good night” is only for saying goodbye at night.

spokenLessons.title: Booking a Doctor's Appointment
spokenLessons.situation: Calling a clinic to book an appointment.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.name: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Good afternoon, City Clinic. How can I help you?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.name: Sunil
dialogue.text: Hello, I'd like to book an appointment with Dr Mehta, please.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.name: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Sure. May I know who's calling?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.name: Sunil
dialogue.text: This is Sunil Rao.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.name: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Thank you, Mr Rao. Is Thursday at 11 a.m. okay for you?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.name: Sunil
dialogue.text: Yes, that works. Thanks a lot.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.name: Receptionist
dialogue.text: You're welcome. See you on Thursday. Goodbye!

phrases.phrase: I'd like to book an appointment.
phrases.meaning: Polite way to ask for a time to visit.
Polite way to ask the caller's name.
How you say your name on the phone.

phrases.phrase: Could you hold for a moment?

vocabulary.meaning: a fixed time to meet someone

activity: Role-play the call with a friend. Swap roles.
Practise saying your phone number in pairs of digits: 98-76-54-32-10.

spokenLessons.title: Buying Clothes
spokenLessons.situation: Shopping for a shirt in a clothing store.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.name: Shopkeeper
dialogue.text: Hello! Are you looking for anything in particular?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.name: Neha
dialogue.text: Yes, I'm looking for a cotton shirt. Do you have this in medium?

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.name: Shopkeeper
dialogue.text: Yes, here you go. The trial room is on the left.

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.name: Neha
dialogue.text: It fits well. How much is it?

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.name: Shopkeeper
dialogue.text: It's 899 rupees.

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.name: Neha
dialogue.text: Is there any discount? Okay, I'll take it. Can I pay by UPI?

phrases.meaning: Ask for another size or colour.

phrases.phrase: How much is it? / How much are these?
Can I pay by card / UPI?

vocabulary.meaning: a room in a shop to try clothes (also: fitting room)

activity: Next time you shop, ask one question in English.
Write five sentences asking for different sizes and colours.

spokenLessons.title: Ordering Food at a Restaurant
spokenLessons.situation: Ordering dinner and asking for the bill.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.name: Waiter
dialogue.text: Good evening! Are you ready to order?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.name: Karan
dialogue.text: Yes, could I have the paneer tikka and two butter rotis, please?

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.name: Waiter
dialogue.text: Sure. Anything to drink?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.name: Karan
dialogue.text: A fresh lime soda, please. Not too sweet.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.name: Waiter
dialogue.text: Of course. It'll be ready in fifteen minutes.

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.name: Karan
dialogue.text: Thanks. And could we get the bill after that?

phrases.phrase: Could we get the bill, please?

vocabulary.meaning: a small dish before the main course
the paper that shows how much to pay (US: check)

activity: Practise ordering your favourite meal out loud.
Learn the names of five dishes in English.

spokenLessons.title: Checking In at the Airport
spokenLessons.situation: Checking in for a domestic flight.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.name: Agent
dialogue.text: Good morning. May I see your ID and booking, please?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.name: Meera
dialogue.text: Here you are. I'm flying to Bengaluru.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.name: Agent
dialogue.text: Thank you. Do you have any bags to check in?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.name: Meera
dialogue.text: Just this one suitcase. Could I have a window seat, please?

blogPosts.title: 10 Common English Mistakes You Should Avoid
blogPosts.excerpt: From “Myself Rahul” to “discuss about”, these everyday errors are easy to fix once you know the correct version.
blogPosts.author: Ananya Deshpande

content.text: Many common mistakes come from translating directly from Hindi, Marathi, Tamil or other languages. The good news: once you notice them, they are easy to fix. Here are ten we hear every week, with the correct version.

items.detail: “Myself” is not used to introduce yourself. Say “I'm Priya” or “My name is Priya”.

items.term: We discussed about the plan. → We discussed the plan.
items.detail: Discuss already includes the meaning of “about”.

items.term: I am having two brothers. → I have two brothers.
items.detail: Have (for possession) is a state verb and isn't used in the continuous.

items.term: He is elder than me. → He is older than me.
items.detail: Use elder only before a noun: my elder brother.

items.term: I will revert back. → I will get back to you.
items.detail: Revert means return to a previous state; “back” repeats the meaning.
We say this morning, this afternoon, tonight.

items.term: She is knowing French. → She knows French.
items.detail: Know is a state verb.

items.term: Return back the book. → Return the book.
items.detail: Return already means give back.

items.term: I passed out of college in 2020. → I graduated in 2020.
items.detail: “Pass out” usually means to faint!

items.term: What is your good name? → May I know your name?
items.detail: “Good name” is a direct translation and sounds unusual to most English speakers.

content.text: Pick two mistakes from this list each week and listen for them in your own speech. Correct yourself out loud.

blogPosts.title: How to Improve Your English Speaking Skills
blogPosts.excerpt: Seven practical habits that build fluency, even if you don't have anyone to practise with.
blogPosts.author: Rohan Mathew

content.text: Speaking is a skill, like cycling or cooking. You improve by doing it, a little every day. These habits work even if you live in a place where you rarely hear English.
1. Shadow native speakers
Play a short clip from a podcast or video. Pause after each sentence and repeat it, copying the rhythm and intonation. Five minutes a day makes a noticeable difference within a month.
2. Think in English
Describe what you're doing in your head: “I'm making tea. I'm adding ginger.” This trains your brain to produce English without translating.
3. Learn phrases, not single words
Learn “make a decision” instead of “decision”, and “pay attention to” instead of “attention”. Phrases come out whole when you speak.
4. Record yourself
Record a one-minute talk about your day. Listen back and note one thing to improve. Keep the recordings to hear your progress.
5. Don't wait to be perfect
Fluency comes before accuracy. Speak, make mistakes, and correct them later. People care more about understanding you than about perfect grammar.
6. Find a speaking partner
A friend, a colleague or an online group. Agree to speak only English for fifteen minutes.
7. Prepare for real situations
Before a phone call, interview or meeting, write down three phrases you will need and practise them out loud.
Start the Spoken English in 30 Days course for a ready-made daily plan.

blogPosts.title: Common English Idioms and Their Meanings
blogPosts.excerpt: Twelve idioms you'll hear at work and with friends, with simple meanings and example sentences.
blogPosts.author: Farah Khan

content.text: Idioms are phrases whose meaning isn't clear from the individual words. Native speakers use them all the time, so knowing the common ones helps you understand conversations, films and emails.

items.detail: Start a conversation in an awkward situation. “He told a joke to break the ice.”
Very easy. “The test was a piece of cake.”
Agreeing or understanding together. “Let's meet so we're all on the same page.”

items.term: Hit the nail on the head
items.detail: Say exactly the right thing. “You hit the nail on the head.”
Stop working. “It's 7 p.m. Let's call it a day.”
Feeling a little ill. “I'm a bit under the weather today.”
Very rarely. “We eat out once in a blue moon.”
Start again. “The plan failed, so we're back to square one.”

items.term: Cost an arm and a leg
items.detail: Be very expensive. “That phone cost an arm and a leg.”
Learn how to do something. “You'll get the hang of it soon.”
Avoid saying something directly. “Stop beating around the bush.”

items.term: Let the cat out of the bag
items.detail: Reveal a secret by mistake. “She let the cat out of the bag about the party.”

content.text: Use idioms in informal speech, but keep them out of formal writing like reports and applications.

blogPosts.title: Since vs For: The Simple Rule
blogPosts.excerpt: Two small words that cause big confusion. One rule fixes it forever.
blogPosts.author: Ananya Deshpande

content.text: Both since and for are used with the present perfect to talk about how long something has continued. The difference is simple.

items.detail: since 2019, since Monday, since 8 a.m., since I was a child
for three years, for two hours, for a long time, for ages

items: I have lived here for seven years.
She has been waiting since 10 o'clock.
She has been waiting for an hour.

content.text: Ask yourself: can I point to it on a calendar or clock? If yes, use since.

content.text: Most learners forget new words within a week. That's not a memory problem; it's a method problem. Try this instead.

items: Learn five words a day, not fifty.
Say each word out loud and copy the stress.
Write one sentence about your own life with each word.
Review after 1 day, 3 days, 7 days and 21 days.
Use the word in a real conversation or message within a week.
